metadata.title: ENDOCRINOLOGY OSCE
metadata.subtitle: 15 Evidence-Corrected Stations
metadata.audienceAndScoring: Final-Year MBBS • 10 minutes per station • 20-point analytic checklist
metadata.facultyNote: This manual contains exactly 15 standalone final-year MBBS endocrinology OSCE stations. Stations 1–6 are clinically revised versions of the supplied topics; stations 7–15 broaden coverage across adrenal, pituitary, calcium, and endocrine emergencies. Local protocols supersede imported guidance. NICE, JBDS, Society for Endocrinology, Endocrine Society, and ADA recommendations are used as identified evidence standards. They do not create Pakistani legal, licensing, prescribing, referral, or service obligations. Faculty must replace imported operational details with the current approved institutional, provincial, and national protocols before summative use. Resource constraints may shape implementation but must not reduce emergency safety.
assessmentDesign: Each station is designed for 10 minutes and uses a 20-point analytic checklist (10 observable items scored 0, 1, or 2).
Score 2 = clearly and independently achieved; 1 = partially achieved or achieved only after a standard prompt; 0 = omitted, incorrect, or unsafe.
The analytic score and global rating must be recorded independently. No numerical pass mark is prescribed; use an approved standard-setting process.
Critical safety errors require examiner review and may justify failure when they create material danger. A minor omission alone should not automatically fail a candidate.
Candidate learning notes are intended for release after the station unless faculty deliberately uses the page for formative open-book teaching.
Standardised prompts restore progress without revealing the answer. Record every prompt and apply the same scoring rule to every candidate.
printingAndAssembly: Each station begins on a new page. Candidate-facing material precedes a marked “Examiner confidential” break.
Remove or cover the Learning Note paragraph if the handout is used during a summative station.
Verify medicines, emergency charts, laboratory reference ranges, referral contacts, and equipment against the local site before use.

stations.title: Hypothyroidism
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, thyroid-test interpretation, and safe treatment explanation
candidateInstructions: You are a final-year MBBS student in a general medical clinic. Mr Hamid Saeed, aged 74 years, has ischaemic heart disease and reports lethargy and muscle weakness.
In 10 minutes: take a focused history, review the thyroid-profile handout, explain the likely diagnosis, and outline safe initial management and follow-up.
You do not need to perform a physical examination. Tell the examiner which focused findings you would seek. Do not prescribe a patient-specific levothyroxine dose.
candidateHandout: Presenting problem: progressive lethargy and generalized muscle weakness.
Thyroid profile: TSH is above the laboratory reference range; free T4 is below the laboratory reference range. The pattern has been confirmed on a repeat sample.
Known comorbidity: ischaemic heart disease. The patient is haemodynamically stable and has no acute chest pain, heart failure symptoms, hypothermia, or altered consciousness.
learningNotes: Learning note (release after the station): TSH is the first-line test. Measure FT4 when TSH is abnormal. T3 is not required to diagnose or monitor hypothyroidism. Levothyroxine is standard replacement; older age and ischaemic heart disease require a cautious lower starting strategy with gradual titration. Once stable, NICE recommends annual TSH monitoring.
simulationScript: Opening: “Doctor, I have become very tired and my muscles feel weak.” Speak slowly but remain alert and cooperative.
If allowed to talk: symptoms developed gradually over several months and are affecting usual household and social activities.

If asked: weight has increased; prefers warm weather and feels unusually cold; constipation; dry skin; thinning dry hair; mild hoarseness; sleeps more; mood is low at times but there is no self-harm idea.
Red flags/differentials: no morning shoulder or hip-girdle stiffness lasting over 45 minutes; no melaena; no orthopnoea; no seizure; no confusion.
Past thyroid history: no thyroid surgery, radioiodine, or known thyroid medicine. No recent neck swelling.
Medicines: takes regular prescribed cardiac medicines; no lithium or amiodarone. No herbal thyroid preparation. No known drug allergy.
ICE: thinks ageing may be responsible; worries about worsening heart disease; hopes for an explanation and a safe treatment.
examinerInstructions: Remain silent unless a standard prompt is required. Give the candidate handout at the start.
If the candidate asks for examination findings, state: dry coarse skin, cool peripheries, slow pulse, and delayed ankle-jerk relaxation; no goitre and no decompensated heart failure.
Accept any safe local prescribing plan that explicitly starts cautiously because of age and ischaemic heart disease, uses TSH-guided titration, and avoids an unsupported fixed dose.
Do not award a separate mark for ordering T3. Record prompts. A prompted action may receive a maximum of 1/2 for its checklist item.
keyAnswerGuide: Recognise primary hypothyroidism from high TSH with low FT4, while checking symptoms, functional effect, cardiac status, medicines, prior thyroid treatment, and red flags for severe disease.
Explain that the thyroid gland is underactive and replacement with levothyroxine is usually long term.

Because the patient is older and has ischaemic heart disease, recommend a cautious low-start, slow-titration approach under the treating clinician/local formulary; monitor for angina, palpitations, or heart-failure symptoms.
Recheck TSH after dose changes at the guideline/local-protocol interval until stable; once stable, monitor annually under NICE NG145. Avoid routine T3 monitoring.
suggestedApproach: Open and listen without interruption.
Clarify the hypothyroid symptom cluster and functional impact.
Screen cardiac and neurological red flags, alternative explanations, past thyroid treatment, and medicines.
Interpret TSH/FT4 in plain language.
Explain cautious replacement, monitoring, adherence, administration, and safety-netting.
Check understanding and invite questions.

stations.title: Hyperthyroidism
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history and antithyroid-drug safety counselling
candidateInstructions: You are in an outpatient medical clinic. Mrs Abdullah, an adult with asthma, has six months of palpitations, sweating, and hand tremor. A thyroid profile supports hyperthyroidism.
In 10 minutes: take a focused history and counsel her about initial treatment, antithyroid-drug safety, symptom control, and follow-up.
No physical examination is required. Pregnancy status and intentions must be addressed.
candidateHandout: Thyroid profile: TSH below the reference range and FT4 above the reference range.
Past history: asthma requiring inhaled treatment. Current rhythm is regular tachycardia; she is haemodynamically stable.
learningNotes: Learning note: When TSH is low, interpret FT4; measure T3 if TSH is low and FT4 is normal. Carbimazole is commonly used outside the first trimester. PTU is preferred in the first trimester. Fever, sore throat, or mouth ulcers require stopping the antithyroid drug and urgent FBC. Hepatotoxicity symptoms require prompt review. A non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol should be avoided in asthma.
simulationScript: Opening: “My heart races, I sweat a lot, and my hands shake.” Appear worried but not breathless.
If asked: heat intolerance, weight loss despite good appetite, frequent stools, poor sleep, and difficulty writing because hands are moist and tremulous.
Cardiorespiratory: no chest pain, fainting, orthopnoea, or ankle swelling. Asthma wheezes episodically; propranolol has not been prescribed.
Eye/neck: gritty eyes but no double vision or visual loss; has noticed mild neck fullness without pain.
Pregnancy: not currently pregnant; would like pregnancy in the future and is willing to discuss timing and contraception with the specialist team.
Medicines: inhalers only; no amiodarone, lithium, thyroid hormone, or iodine-containing supplement. No known drug allergy.
ICE: fears a heart problem; wants rapid symptom relief without worsening asthma.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. If asked for examination findings: warm moist hands, fine tremor, regular tachycardia, diffuse non-tender goitre, no heart failure, and no visual-field deficit.
Accept locally available rate-control alternatives only if the candidate acknowledges asthma, avoids non-selective beta-blockade, and seeks senior/local-guideline advice.
The candidate need not quote a carbimazole dose. Full marks require agranulocytosis advice. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Confirm the thyrotoxic symptom cluster; assess arrhythmia/heart failure, eye disease, neck symptoms, medicines, pregnancy, and impact.

Explain antithyroid therapy and specialist/endocrine follow-up. Carbimazole is a common first-line option outside first-trimester pregnancy; first-trimester treatment requires review and PTU is preferred.

Give explicit written/verbal safety advice: stop the antithyroid drug and obtain urgent assessment/FBC for fever, sore throat, or mouth ulcers; seek prompt review for jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, marked pruritus, or upper abdominal pain.
Do not prescribe propranolol in this asthma case. Select symptom control according to asthma severity, cardiac status, local protocol, and senior review.
Monitor TFTs during treatment; the NICE evidence summary uses 4–8-week review until stable, then 3–6-month intervals.
suggestedApproach: Elicit symptoms and functional effect.
Screen cardiovascular, eye, neurological, and pregnancy red flags.
Review asthma and medicines.
Explain diagnosis and options.
Prioritise antithyroid-drug safety and asthma-safe symptom control.
Agree monitoring and specialist follow-up.

Asks about heat intolerance, weight loss, appetite, bowel habit, sleep, and tremor.
Assesses palpitations, chest pain, syncope, breathlessness, and heart-failure symptoms.

Avoids propranolol in asthma and arranges TFT monitoring/specialist follow-up.

stations.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
stations.primaryCompetency: Individualised treatment planning and shared decision-making
candidateInstructions: You are reviewing Mrs Anam Awais, aged 47 years, who has had type 2 diabetes for two years. Her current random glucose is 300 mg/dL and glycaemic control is above her agreed target.
In 10 minutes: identify contributors and complications, interpret the summary handout, and agree a safe initial management plan.
Do not make unsupported driving-law statements. Use local prescribing policy where it differs from imported guidance.
candidateHandout: Symptoms: thirst, polyuria, nocturia, tiredness, and recurrent skin boils. No vomiting, abdominal pain, or altered consciousness.

Current treatment: metformin; adherence has been inconsistent because of abdominal bloating. Renal function is adequate for the options under discussion. No known heart failure, established cardiovascular disease, or chronic kidney disease is documented.
Monitoring: HbA1c is above the individualised target. Eye screening is overdue. Blood pressure and lipid review are due.
learningNotes: Learning note: Current NICE NG28 treatment is individualised by cardiovascular disease/risk, heart failure, CKD, contraindications, tolerability, access, and preferences. The current pathway supports metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor for many adults when appropriate. During significant vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, or dehydration, withhold metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors and seek advice. SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycaemic DKA.
simulationScript: Opening: “I am thirsty, pass urine often, and feel less energetic.”
If asked: increased appetite but some weight loss; recurrent boils; genital itching; blurred vision intermittently; tingling in toes; no foot wound.
Adherence: often misses metformin because of bloating and work; does not use herbal remedies. No drug allergy.
Lifestyle: irregular meals, sugary drinks, little exercise. Does not smoke; no harmful alcohol use.
Complications/comorbidity: no chest pain, stroke symptoms, orthopnoea, known kidney disease, or pregnancy. Blood pressure has been high previously.
Psychosocial/ICE: work and family stress interfere with self-care; worries about complications; wants a practical affordable plan.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. The candidate should not be required to quote an HbA1c threshold or a drug dose.

Accept a safe locally available alternative if it is individualised and justified. To receive full safety marks, the candidate must address acute-illness sick-day rules and SGLT2-related DKA warnings if recommending that class.
If rapid improvement is proposed, expect eye/retinopathy review. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Clarify osmotic symptoms, adherence, adverse effects, diet/activity, infection, medicines, psychosocial barriers, hypoglycaemia history, and micro/macrovascular complications.
Exclude acute metabolic decompensation clinically. Review HbA1c, renal function, urine albumin, BP, lipids, eye status, and feet.

Optimise metformin tolerability/adherence, including consideration of modified-release formulation where locally available. Consider adding an SGLT2 inhibitor under the current NICE pathway when appropriate, after discussing benefits, genital infection, volume depletion, sick-day rules, and euglycaemic DKA.

Agree realistic nutrition/activity goals, cardiovascular-risk management, vaccinations according to local policy, and structured follow-up. Individualise glycaemic target and account for affordability.

Screen acute illness and complications.
Review cardiovascular, renal, and eye/foot status.
Agree lifestyle priorities.
Individualise medication using comorbidity, tolerability, access, and preference.

stations.title: Hypoglycaemia
stations.primaryCompetency: Emergency recognition, immediate treatment, and prevention counselling
candidateInstructions: You are seeing Mr Zeeshan, aged 45 years, with type 2 diabetes. Since glimepiride was started, he has had sweating, tremor, dizziness, unsteady gait, and confusion at 3 a.m. and after exercise. Home glucose was below 70 mg/dL during both episodes.
In 10 minutes: demonstrate immediate management for the conscious patient presented, explain what changes if swallowing or consciousness is impaired, and counsel on prevention.
No examination is required.
candidateHandout: Current state: conscious, cooperative, able to swallow; capillary glucose below 70 mg/dL.
Medicines: glimepiride and atenolol. Episodes improve after food. No known drug allergy.
learningNotes: Learning note: For a conscious patient able to swallow, give 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if still below 70 mg/dL, then give longer-acting carbohydrate after recovery. Chocolate and fatty foods are not first-line. Do not give oral treatment if consciousness or swallowing is impaired. Severe hypoglycaemia is defined by need for assistance, not only a glucose value.
simulationScript: Opening: “I am sweating and shaking again. I think the new tablet is causing it.”
Act anxious and mildly tremulous but answer appropriately and swallow safely.
If asked: episodes followed a missed/late meal and vigorous exercise; no insulin use; no vomiting or renal diagnosis known.
Hypertension: takes atenolol. Explain that palpitations are not always prominent during episodes.
Lifestyle: smokes; drinks alcohol regularly; wants help to reduce both.
ICE: fears permanent brain damage and expects a safer medication plan.
examinerInstructions: Provide a simulated glucose meter result below 70 mg/dL. The candidate should verbalise 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate and a 15-minute recheck.
When asked what happens after treatment, state that symptoms improve and repeat glucose is above 70 mg/dL.

Do not require a specific replacement diabetes medicine. Expect urgent medication review, assessment of renal/liver function and meal/activity pattern, and caution that beta-blockers can mask warning symptoms.
Oral carbohydrate in an unconscious patient is a material safety failure.
keyAnswerGuide: Recognise symptomatic level-1 hypoglycaemia and treat before prolonged history-taking.

Give 15 g rapid carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then longer-acting carbohydrate once recovered. Observe longer and seek medical review because sulfonylurea-related hypoglycaemia can recur.
If unable to swallow or unconscious: protect airway, call for help, place safely, use local emergency glucagon/IV glucose pathway, monitor glucose and recovery, and do not give anything orally.

Review glimepiride urgently; assess meals, exercise, alcohol, kidney/liver function, and medicines. Provide glucose-monitoring, rapid-carbohydrate, identification, family education, and locally applicable driving advice.
suggestedApproach: Treat immediately.
Recheck at 15 minutes and complete recovery treatment.
Assess cause and recurrence risk.
Explain the impaired-consciousness pathway.
Arrange medication review and prevention plan.
Address the patient’s fear and check understanding.

checklist.criterion: Recognises hypoglycaemia and prioritises immediate treatment.
Confirms consciousness and ability to swallow before oral treatment.
Gives 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate rather than chocolate/milk as first treatment.
Rechecks capillary glucose after 15 minutes.

stations.title: Diabetic Foot
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused foot assessment, risk recognition, and urgent referral planning
candidateInstructions: You are assessing Mr Ramazan Ahmad, aged 55 years, with type 2 diabetes and a plantar foot ulcer present for three weeks.
In 10 minutes: describe a focused diabetic foot examination using the supplied findings, identify the active problems and urgency, and explain immediate management and prevention.
A manikin is available. Verbalise painful or invasive steps and obtain consent.
candidateHandout: Diabetes control is above target. The patient is a heavy smoker.

Right foot: plantar ulcer over a pressure point; loss of protective sensation on 10 g monofilament; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are not palpable; foot is cooler than the other side. No pus, spreading erythema, systemic illness, or fever is present. Ulcer depth is not yet fully defined.
learningNotes: Learning note: Assess perfusion, neuropathy, infection, site, area, and depth. Limb- or life-threatening disease needs immediate escalation. Under NICE NG19, other active diabetic foot problems require specialist foot-service referral within one working day. Antibiotics are for clinical infection, not for every ulcer. Consider acute Charcot neuroarthropathy when there is redness, warmth, swelling, or deformity.
simulationScript: Opening: “This wound under my foot has not healed, and walking is difficult.”
Ulcer: noticed three weeks ago; little pain; no discharge, smell, fever, or rapidly spreading redness; no previous ulcer or amputation.
Neuropathy/ischaemia: numb toes, sometimes night discomfort; no rest pain reported. Feet often feel cold.
Foot care: sometimes walks barefoot; checks feet irregularly; shoes are tight at the forefoot.
Medicines: metformin and an antihypertensive; no ulcer antibiotic; no allergy.
ICE: worries about job loss and amputation; wants to know whether dressing alone is enough.
examinerInstructions: Give the findings card at the start. Do not require a numeric SINBAD score because ulcer area and depth are incompletely supplied.

Expect the candidate to call this an active neuro-ischaemic diabetic foot ulcer requiring prompt multidisciplinary foot-service and vascular assessment. Immediate hospital escalation is required if deterioration suggests limb- or life-threatening infection/ischaemia.
Do not reward empirical antibiotics in the absence of clinical infection. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Inspect both feet, footwear, skin, nails, deformity, pressure points, ulcer site/area/depth, discharge, erythema, warmth, swelling, and possible Charcot change.

Palpate temperature and pulses; assess capillary refill as appropriate; use monofilament plus another sensory modality; consider ankle reflexes. Do not probe an ulcer casually; a trained probe-to-bone assessment and imaging are considered if osteomyelitis is suspected.

Identify neuropathy plus impaired perfusion. Arrange prompt multidisciplinary diabetic-foot referral (NICE: within one working day) and vascular assessment; offload pressure and provide appropriate wound care. Escalate immediately for sepsis, gangrene, critical ischaemia, deep infection, or rapid progression.
Optimise glycaemia and cardiovascular risk; support smoking cessation; give practical daily foot-care and footwear advice.
suggestedApproach: Consent, expose, and compare both feet.
Look: footwear, deformity, skin, ulcer, infection, Charcot features.
Feel: temperature and perfusion.
Test protective sensation safely.
Classify the active problem and urgency.
Offload, refer, optimise risk, educate, and safety-net.

checklist.criterion: Obtains consent, checks pain, exposes appropriately, and compares both feet.
Inspects footwear, skin, nails, interdigital spaces, deformity, pressure points, and ulcer characteristics.
Looks specifically for infection, gangrene, ischaemia, and acute Charcot features.
Assesses temperature, dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses, and perfusion.

Recognises immediate limb/life-threatening escalation criteria.
Arranges prompt multidisciplinary foot-team and vascular assessment; NICE standard is within one working day for other active problems.
Provides offloading/wound-care plan and avoids antibiotics without clinical infection.

stations.title: Gestational Diabetes
candidateInstructions: You are in an antenatal medical clinic. Mrs Abdullah is 24 weeks pregnant and has come to discuss a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).
In 10 minutes: interpret the result, explain the immediate plan and pregnancy treatment principles, address her recent ACE-inhibitor exposure, and arrange postpartum follow-up.
Use the candidate handout. Do not imply that one medication pathway applies to every woman.
candidateHandout: Current 75 g OGTT at 24 weeks: 2-hour plasma glucose 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L). Earlier OGTT at 16 weeks was normal.
Risk factors: previous gestational diabetes; previous baby weighed more than 4.5 kg; BMI above 30 kg/m²; mother had gestational diabetes.
A few days ago, another clinician started lisinopril for raised blood pressure before learning of the pregnancy.
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE NG3 diagnoses gestational diabetes at fasting glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L or 2-hour glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L. Management includes diet, activity, glucose monitoring, and prompt joint obstetric-diabetes review. Medication follows the NG3 pathway and individual findings; metformin and insulin are options. Arrange fasting plasma glucose 6–13 weeks after birth, not a routine postpartum OGTT under NICE.
simulationScript: Opening: “I was told my sugar test is high. Will it harm my baby?”
Current symptoms: feels well; no vomiting, abdominal pain, reduced fetal movement, headache, visual symptoms, or acute illness.
Obstetric history: confirms previous gestational diabetes and a baby over 4.5 kg. No known diabetes outside pregnancy.
Medicine: started lisinopril a few days ago and has taken it as prescribed; no allergy.
Lifestyle: willing to meet a dietitian and monitor glucose. Has family support.
ICE: worries about congenital harm, a very large baby, injections, and future diabetes.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Expect diagnosis using the explicitly supplied NICE thresholds, while noting these are UK evidence standards and local obstetric protocols govern care in Pakistan.
The candidate should advise stopping the ACE inhibitor and arranging prompt obstetric/medical review for a pregnancy-safe blood-pressure plan; do not require a replacement drug or dose.
Accept metformin and/or insulin discussion only as an individualised specialist plan. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Explain that the 2-hour glucose exceeds the cited NICE diagnostic threshold for gestational diabetes.

Arrange prompt review by the joint obstetric-diabetes team because the value is markedly abnormal and risk factors are present. Begin diet/activity support and home glucose monitoring; assess maternal BP and fetal growth/wellbeing according to local protocol.
Stop lisinopril and obtain prompt obstetric/medical review. Reassure without claiming zero risk; document timing and exposure.

Medication must follow the individualised NG3/local pathway, considering glucose profile, contraindications, pregnancy features, preferences, and access. After birth, stop pregnancy-specific therapy as clinically appropriate and arrange fasting plasma glucose at 6–13 weeks plus ongoing diabetes-risk surveillance.
suggestedApproach: Acknowledge concern and confirm pregnancy context.
Interpret OGTT with the supplied threshold.
Assess immediate maternal/fetal concerns and refer promptly.
Explain lifestyle, monitoring, and individualised medication options.
Address ACE-inhibitor exposure safely.
Plan delivery/postpartum transition and long-term surveillance.

checklist.criterion: Explains the OGTT result clearly and checks understanding.
Correctly applies the supplied NICE 2-hour threshold and diagnoses gestational diabetes.

Recommend steroid emergency identification/card, medical-alert identification, spare supplies, travel planning, and family training in emergency injection where locally available.

learningNotes: Learning note: Treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM and rapid 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation. Investigations must not delay treatment. Monitor glucose, electrolytes, fluid status, and response; identify and treat the precipitant.

keyAnswerGuide: Recognise adrenal crisis and begin A–E resuscitation, monitoring, IV access, and senior/emergency support.

Search for and treat a precipitant such as infection. Continue protocol-based glucocorticoid/fluids and transition only under specialist guidance.

candidateInstructions: You are assessing an adult referred with possible Cushing syndrome.

candidateHandout: Observed features: wide purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, and severe hypertension. Generalised obesity is also present.
Medication review supplied after you ask: no oral, injected, inhaled, topical, or traditional preparation containing a known glucocorticoid has been identified.

Specialist screening summary: two recommended first-line cortisol screening tests are reported by the laboratory as abnormal. ACTH and cause-localising investigations have not yet been completed. No adrenal or pituitary imaging has been performed.
learningNotes: Learning note: Discriminating features include proximal myopathy, wide purple striae, easy bruising, and severe hypertension. Exclude exogenous glucocorticoids first. simulationScript: Opening: “My muscles are weak, I bruise easily, and my blood pressure has become difficult to control.”
If asked: difficulty rising from a chair; skin bruises with minor knocks; mood and sleep have worsened; no acute psychosis or infection symptoms.
Steroid exposure: denies prescribed tablets/injections/inhalers/creams and has brought all medicines for review; no known steroid-containing product identified.
Complications: hypertension; increased glucose on recent testing; no known fracture or renal stone.
ICE: worries about cancer; wants a scan immediately.
examinerInstructions: Candidate should verbalise a focused general, skin, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, endocrine, and neurological examination with dignity.
The handout deliberately gives interpreted abnormal screening results without thresholds. Expect ACTH-guided specialist localisation and assessment of complications before definitive treatment.
Accept a safe alternative biochemical sequence consistent with specialist/local protocol.
keyAnswerGuide: Look for discriminatory features rather than diagnosing from obesity alone. Examine BP, skin/striae/bruising, proximal power, fat distribution, infection, virilisation where relevant, spine/fracture clues, mood/cognition, and visual fields if pituitary disease is suspected.
Review all routes of exogenous glucocorticoid exposure before labelling endogenous disease.
Interpret the two abnormal screens as requiring endocrine confirmation and cause evaluation. Measure ACTH and use specialist dynamic testing/localisation; image only after biochemical direction.

Assess and manage complications such as hypertension, diabetes, infection risk, osteoporosis, thrombotic risk, and psychiatric effects. Refer to an endocrine multidisciplinary team; surgery is principal definitive treatment when an operable causal lesion is confirmed.

stations.title: Acute Symptomatic Hypocalcaemia
stations.primaryCompetency: Emergency recognition and monitored IV calcium treatment
candidateInstructions: You are called to an adult who developed perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, and stridor after neck surgery.
In 10 minutes: lead immediate assessment and management, including treatment and monitoring.
Verbalise medication orders to the nurse/examiner.
candidateHandout: A–E: airway threatened by stridor; breathing spontaneous; circulation currently maintained; patient has painful carpopedal spasm. ECG shows prolonged QT. Serum calcium is below the laboratory reference range.
learningNotes: Learning note: Severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia requires airway/senior support and 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10–20 minutes with ECG monitoring. Reassess symptoms and calcium; investigate/correct the cause and associated electrolyte abnormalities according to local protocol.
simulationScript: Nurse opening: “This patient has tingling, hand spasm, and noisy breathing after neck surgery.”
If asked: symptoms developed rapidly; no prior seizure. The patient is frightened and struggles to speak because of stridor.
After airway help and monitored calcium are ordered: state that anaesthesia/senior help arrives, ECG monitoring is attached, and calcium treatment starts.
If the candidate delays: stridor worsens; provide the emergency stall prompt.
examinerInstructions: Act as the nurse. Expect immediate A–E, airway/anaesthetic support, ECG monitoring, and IV calcium gluconate.
Award the treatment item only if the candidate specifies 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate over 10–20 minutes and monitoring.
Accept further infusion/replacement only according to local protocol with repeat calcium and cause correction. Prompted actions score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Recognise severe symptomatic postoperative hypocalcaemia with laryngospasm/stridor, tetany, and prolonged QT.
Call for senior/anaesthetic help, assess A–E, support airway and oxygenation as indicated, obtain IV access, and attach ECG monitoring.
Give 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10–20 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring; reassess symptoms, ECG, and calcium. Repeat/infuse only under the emergency/local protocol.
Investigate cause and associated abnormalities, including magnesium as locally indicated, and coordinate surgical/endocrine management.
suggestedApproach: Recognise airway-threatening hypocalcaemia.
Call for anaesthetic/senior help and perform A–E.
Attach ECG and secure IV access.
Give monitored IV calcium gluconate.
Reassess and continue protocol-based correction.
Investigate postoperative cause and associated electrolytes.

checklist.criterion: Recognises severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia from tetany/stridor and prolonged QT.
Calls for senior/anaesthetic/resuscitation help immediately.
Uses an A–E approach and prioritises airway support.
Applies ECG monitoring and obtains IV access.
Orders 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV.
Specifies administration over 10–20 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring.
Reassesses airway, symptoms, ECG, and calcium after treatment.
Uses local protocol for repeat dosing/infusion rather than unmonitored empiricism.
Investigates the postoperative cause and relevant associated electrolytes, including magnesium where indicated.
Coordinates ongoing surgical/endocrine care and documents the emergency response.

stations.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
stations.primaryCompetency: Protocol-based resuscitation, insulin, potassium, and monitoring
candidateInstructions: You are the first doctor assessing an adult with diabetes who has vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, and deep rapid breathing.
In 10 minutes: interpret the DKA criteria card and lead initial management and monitoring using the supplied protocol summary.
Verbalise orders to the nurse/examiner. Do not stop insulin solely because glucose falls while ketoacidosis persists.
candidateHandout: Diagnostic card (JBDS adult standard): glucose >11 mmol/L or known diabetes; blood ketones >3 mmol/L or urine ketones >2+; venous pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L. This patient meets all three components.

Initial state: clinically dehydrated with Kussmaul respiration; potassium has been measured before insulin and is within the laboratory reference range. No shock or focal neurological deficit is present.

Protocol summary: begin protocol-based IV 0.9% sodium chloride; fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour; monitor and replace potassium according to the approved chart; monitor glucose, ketones, venous acid–base status, electrolytes, fluid balance, and clinical response; add glucose-containing fluid when the protocol indicates while continuing insulin for ketone clearance; identify and treat the precipitant.
learningNotes: Learning note: DKA care is fluids plus fixed-rate insulin plus potassium management, monitoring, and precipitant treatment. Neurological deterioration is uncommon but serious and requires urgent escalation.
simulationScript: Nurse opening: “The patient with diabetes has been vomiting and is breathing deeply. The DKA criteria card is positive.”
If asked: insulin was missed during a febrile illness; no chest pain or pregnancy information is supplied.
After initial orders: IV access and monitoring are established. Repeat results are available only when the candidate requests them.
If the candidate stops insulin when glucose falls: ketones and acidosis remain abnormal.
examinerInstructions: Act as the nurse. The candidate may use the supplied JBDS criteria and protocol summary; threshold recall beyond the card is not assessed.
Expect A–E, senior support, fluids, fixed-rate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour after potassium assessment, potassium replacement by chart, and frequent reassessment.
Accept concurrent continuation of appropriate long-acting basal insulin if stated as local/JBDS protocol, but do not require it for a checklist mark.
Escalate the simulation for shock, altered consciousness, failure to improve, or other severe features if the candidate asks.
keyAnswerGuide: Recognise DKA using the supplied triad and assess severity with A–E, observations, mental state, hydration, and comorbidity.
Call for senior help, establish monitoring/IV access, and begin protocol-based 0.9% sodium chloride. Start fixed-rate IV insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour after potassium assessment.

Monitor potassium closely and replace according to the approved chart. Check glucose, ketones, venous pH/bicarbonate, electrolytes, renal function, fluid input/output, and clinical response at protocol intervals.

When glucose reaches the protocol trigger, add glucose-containing fluid but continue insulin until ketone/acidosis resolution criteria are met. Identify and treat infection, missed insulin, myocardial ischaemia, drugs, or other precipitants as applicable.
Escalate haemodynamic instability, neurological deterioration, severe electrolyte disturbance, or failure to improve.
suggestedApproach: Recognise DKA and assess severity.
Call for help; monitoring and IV access.
Start isotonic fluid protocol.
Check potassium, then fixed-rate insulin.
Monitor ketones, acid–base status, glucose, potassium, and fluid balance.
Treat precipitant and escalate non-response/instability.

checklist.criterion: Recognises DKA using the supplied glucose/diabetes, ketone, and acidosis criteria.
Uses A–E, assesses hydration/mental state, and calls for senior help.
Establishes IV access, cardiac/physiological monitoring, and baseline investigations.
Starts protocol-based IV 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation.

Monitors glucose, ketones, venous pH/bicarbonate, electrolytes, renal function, and fluid balance.
Adds glucose-containing fluid when indicated while continuing insulin until ketoacidosis resolves.
Identifies/treats the precipitant and escalates instability, neurological decline, or failure to improve.
